summary: Describes the External Data Representation (XDR) standard, a way to write data in a form independent of the machine, as it is deployed and accepted. It replaces RFC 1832. It is an Internet Standard.

plainLanguage.summary: XDR defines a common way to describe and encode data so computers with different architectures can interpret it consistently. It uses fixed rules for numbers, structures, and variable-length values.

subtitle: A shared language and byte encoding for exchanging data between different computer architectures.

tldr.problem: Different computer architectures can represent data differently, so exchanging raw memory does not give a consistent result.
tldr.mechanism: XDR describes data with a C-like language and encodes values in a consistent byte order using four-byte units and zero fill where needed.
tldr.outcome: RFC 4506 is an Internet Standard that obsoletes RFC 1832 without technical changes to the XDR specification.

today: RFC 4506 is an Internet Standard that obsoletes RFC 1832. Its text states that it makes no technical changes to RFC 1832.

sections.title: What XDR Describes
sections.content:
External Data Representation (XDR) is a standard for describing and encoding data exchanged between computer architectures. Its language describes data formats; it is not a programming language. Protocols such as ONC RPC and NFS use XDR to describe their data.

XDR assumes that bytes, defined as 8 bits, can be carried between devices without losing their meaning. It uses implicit typing, so the format description supplies the expected type rather than adding a type label to every encoded value.
sections.plainLanguage: XDR gives different computers shared rules for reading exchanged data. Its language describes the data's format rather than running instructions.

sections.title: Four-Byte Units and Padding
sections.content:
Every XDR item occupies a multiple of four bytes. If a value does not fill the last four-byte unit, it is followed by 0 to 3 zero bytes. Bytes appear in a defined order in the stream, so the same data has the same representation across machines.

All XDR numeric values use the same byte order, with the most significant byte first. RFC 4506 explains that the four-byte unit balances alignment needs against encoded size.
sections.plainLanguage: XDR arranges data in groups of four bytes. It fills any unused space at the end with zero bytes.

sections.title: Numbers and Floating-Point Values
sections.content:
An XDR signed integer is a 32-bit two's-complement value; an unsigned integer is also 32 bits. Hyper integers use 64 bits. Enumerations use the signed integer representation, and encoding a value not assigned in the enumeration is an error.

XDR defines float, double, and quadruple floating-point representations based on IEEE formats. They use 32, 64, and 128 bits respectively. A NaN is system-dependent and must not be interpreted as anything other than NaN.
sections.plainLanguage: XDR assigns fixed sizes and representations to integer and floating-point values. A reader can use those rules instead of relying on the local computer's memory layout.

sections.title: Strings, Opaque Data and Arrays
sections.content:
Opaque data is a sequence of bytes that XDR does not interpret. Variable-length opaque data and strings begin with a 32-bit length, followed by the bytes and any zero fill needed to reach a four-byte boundary. Strings contain ASCII bytes, and their declared maximum length must not be exceeded.

A variable-length array starts with its element count and then encodes each element in order. Fixed-length arrays encode their elements in order without an element count. Every element type is defined in the data description.
sections.plainLanguage: For a variable-length value, XDR writes its length before its contents. It adds zero bytes when needed to reach the next four-byte boundary.

sections.title: Structures, Unions and the XDR Language
sections.content:
A structure encodes its declared components in order. A discriminated union encodes a value called the discriminant, followed by the selected arm. If there is no default arm, values not listed in the declaration are invalid. Optional data uses a Boolean value to indicate whether the following item is present.

The XDR language is specified using an extended Backus-Naur Form. It uses declarations for types such as integers, strings, arrays, structures, and unions. RFC 4506 includes a file description and shows its encoded bytes.
sections.plainLanguage: A structure stores its parts in a defined order. A union stores a selector first, so the reader knows which part follows.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
XDR is a data description language, not a protocol, so protocols that carry XDR data must provide any needed security services. Encoders and decoders still need checks that prevent unsafe data processing.

The RFC identifies risks such as buffer overflows from excessive lengths, embedded zero bytes in strings, characters that are invalid for an application, and very long recursive structures. Decoders should check sizes and avoid unbounded recursive processing.
sections.plainLanguage: XDR does not protect data in transit. Programs that read XDR data must check its lengths and contents before using it.
